pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Changing Shapes of Solids

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "find out how the shapes of solid objects made from some materials can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching." Non-statutory guidance links this to identifying material uses and to Working Scientifically enquiry ('performing simple tests'; 'observing closely'; 'gathering and recording data').

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to reshaping solids by squashing/bending/twisting/stretching — it is a UK-led KS1 objective. The nearest is DCI PS1.A ('Different properties are suited to different purposes') and the K–2 investigation practice; the reshaping-and-identity idea also foreshadows 2-PS1-3 (an object's pieces can be rearranged, the matter persists).

- **Operational details:** Teach the four actions with precise, embodied definitions (squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change shape), then run first-hand comparative tests on a deliberately varied set of materials — playdough/plasticine, sponge, elastic band, paper, a wooden stick, a stone — so children see that materials respond DIFFERENTLY. Use a predict-then-test sequence to surface ideas before handling. Crucially, keep the enquiry on the MATERIAL an object is made from (not the object), and make the identity point explicit: the shape changes but the material stays the same stuff. Include materials that keep their new shape (dough) and ones that spring back (elastic) so the contrast is unavoidable.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can demonstrate all four actions, compare how two materials respond (clay squashes and stays; wood barely bends), and state that the material is still the same material after its shape has changed — without over-claiming that everything springs back.
bestPractices: Define each action precisely and let children embody it (turn their hands to 'twist', pull to 'stretch') before testing materials.
Use predict-then-test: children predict how each material will respond, then test by hand, so the misconception surfaces and is confronted by evidence.
Deliberately include BOTH spring-back materials (elastic band, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire) so 'everything is elastic' cannot survive.
Keep the enquiry framed on the MATERIAL, not the object — 'we are testing what it is made of' — reinforcing objects-vs-materials.
Make the identity point explicit: changing the shape does not change what material it is; no new material is made.
Record results in a simple table (material × does it keep its shape?) to support the classify/compare Working Scientifically skill.
keyRepresentations: A varied materials tray: playdough, sponge, elastic band, paper, wooden stick, stone, soft wire
Embodied action cards for squash / bend / twist / stretch
A predict-then-test recording grid (material down the side; springs back? stays changed? can't change?)
Side-by-side contrast of an elastic band (returns) and a lump of dough (stays)
A 'same material, new shape' before/after pair emphasising the material is unchanged
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalised elasticity — assuming ALL objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will spring back to their original shape (the central Y2 misconception).
Believing a physical shape change cannot be undone at all — or conversely that it always can.
Thinking that changing an object's shape changes the material it is made of (it does not — no new material forms).
Testing the OBJECT rather than the material, so results are attributed to the item ('the spoon') not the substance ('metal').
Assuming a rigid material (wood, stone) simply hasn't been pushed hard enough, rather than that some materials do not change shape this way.

learn.summary: For children aged 6-7, teach how the shapes of solid objects can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching, with the key insight that materials respond DIFFERENTLY: some spring back (elastic), some keep the new shape (plastic/permanent), and some barely change this way (rigid). Keep the enquiry on the MATERIAL an object is made from, and make explicit that changing the shape does not change what the material is and makes no new material. The central misconception to confront is over-generalised elasticity (expecting everything to spring back). The strongest activity lets children apply a force first-hand and then release to witness the spring-back-vs-stay contrast; a hands-on tray of real dough, elastic and sponge is the natural companion, with a screen or picture version as a scaffold that offers a different experience.

activities.title: Materials deformation bench: apply a force, then let go
feedback: When the squeezed sponge springs back but the squeezed dough stays flat, point out the contrast directly: the same action gave different outcomes because they are made of different materials.
If a child predicts the dough will spring back, run the let-go test and let the observed result do the teaching rather than just telling them.
When a child tries to squash the wooden stick (or stone) and it barely moves, name the third case: some materials do not change shape this way when we use our hands.
Reinforce after every trial that the material is still the same — the squashed dough is still dough, the bent wire is still metal.
activities.rationale: Reshaping is a direct, hands-on investigation with a material-dependent outcome, matching the statutory 'find out how the shapes... can be changed' enquiry. Applying a force and then releasing it lets the child witness the spring-back-vs-stay distinction first-hand, which surfaces and confronts the over-generalised-elasticity misconception with evidence. Deliberately including both spring-back materials (elastic, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire), plus a rigid one (wood, stone), is intended to make the contrast unavoidable. A persistent 'still the same material' label keeps the identity idea in view. A screen bench can model release with live recompute; a real tray of dough, elastic and sponge supplies the genuine tactile feel — the two offer different experiences and neither is universally required.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'find out how the shapes of solid objects made from some materials can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching'; non-statutory uses guidance and WS enquiry.

Central Y2 misconception = over-generalised elasticity ('all objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will return to their previous shape'); some materials keep the new shape or cannot be changed; teach that pupils test the material, not the object.
Elastic (recoverable) vs plastic (permanent) deformation — child-accessible physics of why some materials spring back and some stay changed.
learnerActions: Choose a material from a varied set — playdough/plasticine, an elastic band, a sponge, a thick wooden stick or block, a stone, soft wire, paper.
Pick one of the four actions and apply it: press/squeeze to squash, curve it to bend, hold each end and turn opposite ways to twist, pull to stretch.
Watch the material deform as the force is applied (dough flattens, wire coils, elastic thins).
Release ('let go') and observe what happens: does it snap back to its old shape, stay in the new shape, or barely move?
Record the result for each material and the action you used in a comparison grid: springs back / stays changed / won't change this way.
Note each time that the material is still the same stuff — e.g. a tag or label 'this is still WOOD' — so the shape changed but the material did not.
activities.intendedInsight: Materials respond differently to the same action: squeeze a sponge and it springs back, squeeze dough and it stays flattened, and squeeze a thick wooden stick or a stone and it barely changes. Likewise, a stretched elastic band snaps back while twisted soft wire stays twisted. So 'everything springs back' is not true, and the result can depend on the action as well as the material. Across all of this, the material itself is unchanged.

activities.title: Embody and define the four actions
feedback: If a child only pushes/squashes regardless of the instruction, model each of the four actions once with a spare material — this is a procedural gap, so focus on the action, not on material properties.
Confirm the distinct hand movement for each: a twist needs two ends turned opposite ways, a stretch needs a pull.
activities.rationale: Defining each action precisely and letting children embody it establishes the vocabulary and motor procedure that the comparative tests depend on. Treating all four as one generic push is a common procedural gap distinct from the conceptual material-response ideas. A matching/recognition task with audio can support early readers but only checks recognition; actually performing the actions is what elicits the production skill. No row source evidences the embodiment technique itself, so none is cited here.
learnerActions: Learn each action with a precise, embodied definition: squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so it is not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change its shape.
Perform each action with your own hands first (turn your hands to twist, pull to stretch) before touching a material.
Match each action word to a demonstration or picture of that action.
Say the definition aloud (with audio support for pre/early readers).
activities.intendedInsight: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching are four distinct actions, not one generic 'push'. Being able to produce each one distinctly is needed before comparing how materials respond.

activities.title: Predict, then test, and sort by how materials respond
feedback: Where a prediction was wrong (e.g. you expected the clay to spring back), treat the surprise as the learning: the same action gave a different result because the material is different.
Use the completed table to compare two materials side by side — clay squashes and stays; a thick piece of wood barely bends.

If a child says a rigid material just 'wasn't pushed hard enough', agree that a much bigger force might bend or break it, but explain that with the force our hands can give it does not change shape this way — that is what we observed.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-test sequence brings the misconception into the open before handling, so it can be confronted by evidence. Sorting and recording in a table develops the Working Scientifically classify/compare skill. Sorting and matching tasks can assess and score these ideas cleanly, but a linear recall quiz does not itself build the felt contrast — so the sort is paired with real testing.
sourceClaims: Central Y2 misconception = over-generalised elasticity ('all objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will return to their previous shape'); some materials keep the new shape or cannot be changed; teach that pupils test the material, not the object.
Elastic (recoverable) vs plastic (permanent) deformation — child-accessible physics of why some materials spring back and some stay changed.
learnerActions: Before handling each material, predict how it will respond to a chosen action: will it spring back, stay changed, or barely change?
Test your prediction by hand and compare what happened to what you expected.

Sort the materials into three groups for the action you tested (a different action can give a different result): springs back (e.g. squeezed sponge, stretched elastic band), stays changed (e.g. squashed dough, bent soft wire), won't change this way by hand (e.g. squeezed thick wood, stone).
Build a simple table with the material down the side and columns for 'springs back?', 'stays changed?', 'won't change?'.
activities.intendedInsight: Predicting first surfaces your idea so the evidence can confirm or overturn it; recording in a table supports comparing and classifying materials by how they respond.

activities.title: Same material, new shape: show the stuff is unchanged
feedback: If a child says the squashed clay 'isn't clay any more', show it is the same clay, the same weight, and can be rolled back into a ball — only the shape changed.
Connect the weighing result to the idea: nothing was added or removed, so it is the same material with the same weight.
activities.rationale: Making the identity point explicit directly addresses the misconception that reshaping turns the stuff into a different material. Comparing before/after and checking weight gives concrete, observable evidence that the material persists through a shape change. For young learners the weight before and after a simple squash is expected to be the same because no matter is added or removed. This matter-persistence idea is not directly evidenced by the row's sources (it foreshadows later conservation-of-weight ideas such as NGSS 5-PS1-2), so none is cited.
learnerActions: Take a lump of clay, roll it into a ball, then squash it flat — look at the before and after.
Explain whether it is still clay after being squashed, and how you could show it is the same stuff (e.g. roll it back into a ball).
Weigh a ball of clay, squash it, and weigh it again; compare the two weights.
Do the same reasoning for a bent metal paperclip: is it still metal after bending?
activities.intendedInsight: Changing an object's shape does not change the material it is made of and does not make new material — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal, and the weight stays the same because nothing was added or taken away.

constraints: Keep the enquiry framed on the MATERIAL an object is made from ('we are testing what it is made of'), not on the named object, so results are attributed to the substance (metal) and not the item (the spoon).

Deliberately include BOTH spring-back materials (elastic band, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire), plus at least one rigid material (wood, stone), so the over-generalised-elasticity idea is challenged by evidence.

A tap-to-reveal picture or lift-the-flap can name and illustrate the four actions and show before/after, but its spring-back answers are pre-authored: it asserts the outcome rather than letting the child apply the force and witness it. Treat it as a vocabulary scaffold, not a replacement for first-hand testing.

Sorting, matching and prediction multiple-choice can assess and score these ideas but check recognition; recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the felt contrast of applying a force and releasing it.
Pre/early readers need audio scaffolding for definitions and prompts.
A real, tactile tray (dough, elastic, sponge) and a screen model offer different experiences; the real materials supply the genuine feel of squeezing. Neither is presented as universally required.
Avoid over-claiming: do not imply everything springs back, and do not imply a physical shape change can never be undone — some can be reversed (rolling clay back), some cannot easily.
Frame rigid materials (wood, stone) as 'do not change shape this way' at this level rather than as proof they just need more force; keep claims within what a child observes by hand.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (Oak National Academy; Kiddle Deformation) are marked unverified in the original row; the DfE National Curriculum source is marked verified. Evidence strength has not been re-checked.

The DfE source grounds the four named actions and the investigative enquiry (activity 1); it is NOT efficacy evidence for the embodiment/motor-procedure method, so the 'Embody and define' activity cites no source claim.
Activity 4's material-identity-persistence principle is not directly supported by any row source (it foreshadows NGSS 2-PS1-3); sourceClaims left empty there.

The original 3D-interactive note asserted 'genuine spatial depth adds little conceptual value' for this topic; softened here — a side view reads squashing/bending well and tactile work is a complement — without claiming 3D 'adds nothing'.

The original framed the screen bench as doing something 'a static picture cannot supply'; retained only as a narrow affordance (live recompute lets the child witness release), not as a universal law that static images cannot teach this.

The weighing check (NGSS 2-PS1 foreshadowing of matter persisting) assumes a simple reshape with no material added or removed; present it to children as 'nothing added or taken away, so the same weight'.
NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to reshaping solids by these four actions; it is a UK-led KS1 objective (nearest DCI PS1.A and the K-2 investigation practice).

probeDeeper: You bent the paperclip and it stayed; you stretched the band and it went back — why the difference?
Is the squashed clay still clay? How could you show me it's the same stuff?
Can you squash the wooden stick the way you squashed the clay? Why not?
If I weigh the ball of clay, then squash it and weigh it again, will the weight change?
assess.correctAnswer: Produces the four distinct actions; observes that some materials hold the new shape (clay squashed, paperclip bent) while others spring back (elastic band, sponge), and that some barely change (wood); states the material itself is unchanged — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changing the shape changes the material — 'the squashed clay isn't clay any more', bent metal 'became something else'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront on the spot: it's the same clay, same weight, and can be rolled back to a ball; only the shape changed, not the material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After reshaping, denies it is still the same material; treats a new shape as new stuff.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises how materials respond — expects everything to spring back (like the band), or nothing to (like the clay); doesn't separate elastic from permanent change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the let-go test on each and line them up: band and sponge return, clay and bent wire stay — let the contrast do the teaching.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the clay will spring back, or that the stretched band will stay stretched.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats squash/bend/twist/stretch as one generic action — just pushes on everything regardless of the instruction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model each of the four actions once with a spare material; this is a procedural gap, not a conceptual one — don't reteach material properties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only squashes/pushes; cannot demonstrate distinct bending, twisting and stretching.

responseLevels.gap: Applies one generic action (pushing); thinks reshaping makes a new material; cannot compare how different materials respond.
responseLevels.full: Performs all four actions, distinguishes materials that hold the shape from those that spring back, AND states the material itself is unchanged — transferring the idea to a new material.
responseLevels.partial: Performs the four actions and sees shapes change, but doesn't distinguish spring-back from permanent change, or is unsure whether the material stays the same.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a lump of clay, a sponge, an elastic band, a wooden lolly stick and a metal paperclip. Say: 'Try to change each one's shape by squashing, bending, twisting or stretching. Which keep their new shape and which spring back? And for each — after you've changed it, is it still the SAME material?' Watch them work.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching (not asking) reveals three things a verbal answer hides: whether the child can produce all four actions distinctly, whether they distinguish spring-back (elastic) from permanent (plastic) change through the let-go test, and — the key idea — whether they think reshaping turns the stuff into a DIFFERENT material.
